entry.title: Anthropic says large language models enable formal software verification at much larger scale [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Anthropic reports that large language models (LLMs) are making formal software verification feasible on a much larger scale than before. This development could significantly improve the reliability and security of software systems by automating complex verification tasks. The company highlights how LLMs can assist in generating formal proofs and checking software correctness more efficiently, potentially transforming software development and quality assurance processes. This advancement may lead to broader adoption of formal verification techniques across the software industry.

entry.title: NVIDIA releases OpenShell, a secure runtime for autonomous AI agents with kernel-level policy enforcement and formal verification [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
entry.summary: NVIDIA has launched OpenShell, a runtime environment designed to safely manage fleets of autonomous AI agents by enforcing strict access policies on files, system calls, and network connections. OpenShell isolates each agent in a sandbox, controlling their permissions and credentials to prevent unauthorized data or network access while allowing necessary operations like file reading and API calls. OpenShell uses kernel instrumentation to enforce policies at runtime and applies formal verification to review policy changes before they are applied, flagging risky permissions for human approval. The platform supports Linux, macOS on Apple Silicon, and Windows with WSL 2, and integrates with container runtimes and Kubernetes for deployment. It also offers SDKs, agent skills, and extensibility features to facilitate development and management of AI agents in secure environments.

entry.title: Analysis of multiple AI models reveals consensus that humans prioritize social belonging over truth, with loyalty shaping beliefs and moral convictions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A study asked various AI models from ten labs across three countries to provide their most controversial opinions on humans, and all models consistently stated that humans tend to prioritize group loyalty and belonging over truth and principles. The models described human behavior as largely driven by social conformity, with intelligence often used to justify pre-existing loyalties rather than to discover objective truth. The shared perspectives included views that humans are rationalizing animals who use their intellect to win social status and maintain group cohesion, rather than to seek reality clearly. Several models emphasized that moral convictions and beliefs are often expressions of tribal loyalty, and that humans prefer coherent social narratives over fragmented truths. This consensus highlights a common AI interpretation of human social and cognitive behavior rather than an individual model's opinion.

entry.title: Researchers argue AI enables enclosure of the scientific information commons, transforming shared knowledge into private wealth and undermining social systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: This article examines the scientific literature as an "information commons," a shared resource without ownership, and compares it to historical agricultural commons that were enclosed and privatized between 1600 and 1800. The authors argue that AI provides tools that facilitate a similar enclosure of the scientific commons, turning publicly shared knowledge into private assets and disrupting the social frameworks that support open access. The paper draws on economic and political frameworks from the history of common lands to analyze how AI-enabled enclosure differs from physical enclosure but shares its core effects. It highlights concerns that this process could represent not just a rapid appropriation of resources but a fundamental challenge to the collaborative nature of scientific knowledge and the systems that sustain it.

entry.title: Canva launches Craft, an AI image model that plans designs before generating images with up to 2K resolution and over 30 aspect ratios [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Canva has introduced Craft, its first in-house AI image generation model that uses a two-stage process to plan designs before creating images, aiming for improved precision, consistency, and control. The model supports up to 2K resolution and more than 30 aspect ratios, enabling the creation of social media posts, marketing content, realistic scenes, and digital art. Canva trained Craft on millions of human-made templates from its content library and ranks it fourth on Design Arena's AI image generation leaderboard. The company emphasizes robust moderation, privacy, and safety controls, and plans to integrate AI agents via the open Model Context Protocol. Craft is now available globally to all Canva users through the Dream Lab feature.

entry.title: Meta's pursuit of AI investment draws sharp criticism from Wall Street analysts and investors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Meta's recent efforts to raise substantial capital for artificial intelligence initiatives have met with skepticism and concern from Wall Street analysts and investors. The criticism highlights doubts about Meta's strategic approach to AI funding and raises questions about the broader market impact of its investment plans.

entry.title: 1Password launches '1Password for Agents' to let AI agents log into user accounts without accessing passwords [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: 1Password has introduced a new feature called 1Password for Agents that enables AI agents to log into users' personal accounts without ever seeing their passwords. The system uses a unique digital key to verify the agent's identity and requires user confirmation before granting access, allowing the agent to fill in credentials securely and perform tasks on the user's behalf. The platform supports various AI agents including Claude Duet from Anthropic, OpenAI's Dots and ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta's Muse, and others, with plans to expand further. This launch comes amid growing concerns about AI agents accessing sensitive accounts, as financial institutions have reported detecting agentic activity in user accounts, raising security and control issues for consumers and banks alike.

entry.title: Microsoft says its GPT-5-powered Diagnostic Orchestrator AI tool achieves 83% accuracy on medical case reports, outperforming generalist physicians [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
entry.summary: Microsoft unveiled a Diagnostic Orchestrator AI tool powered by GPT-5 that scored 83 percent diagnostic accuracy on New England Journal of Medicine case reports, surpassing generalist physicians who scored between 22 and 47 percent depending on case type. The company is positioning this AI to take a leading role in high-stakes diagnostic workflows, prompting hospitals and vendors to reconsider clinical decision-support systems and partnerships.

entry.title: OpenAI launches Decisions API with GPT-6 Luna for faster, cost-effective real-time decision-making in applications [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: OpenAI has made the Decisions API generally available, enabling applications and agents to make fast, focused decisions using GPT-6 Luna. The API supports text, images, and structured inputs, delivering up to 10 times faster responses than the GPT-6 Luna Responses API while reducing latency and cost. Since its public beta, the Decisions API has added features like native GPT-Live integration, prompt caching, and inference residency in the US and EU. It supports three answer types-probability, choice, and score-allowing developers to tailor decision-making to various workflows. Early adopters across OpenAI and customers like Box, Datadog, and Sierra report significant speed improvements and cost savings without sacrificing accuracy. The API also integrates with GPT-Live to enhance real-time voice applications, enabling dynamic decision-making during live conversations such as routing requests or adjusting avatar expressions. This positions the Decisions API as a versatile tool for improving responsiveness and efficiency in diverse application scenarios.

entry.title: Analysis finds AI writing remains wordy and unnatural despite advances, struggling with flow and human-like style as detection tools improve [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Despite rapid progress in AI capabilities for math and coding, AI-generated prose continues to lack the natural flow and functional word choice characteristic of quality human writing. Evaluations of leading models like Opus and Astra reveal persistent issues with wordiness and a forced style that fails to convincingly mimic human patterns. Detection tools such as Pangram have become increasingly effective at identifying AI-written content, narrowing the window when AI could evade detection. The challenges stem partly from AI's tendency to overcorrect and hedge, producing bloated text that contrasts with the circuitous and often unsaid nature of human thought. Additionally, the commercial focus on AI for coding and math rather than prose may have limited investment in improving AI writing quality. Writing requires not only idea generation but also organization and stylistic nuance, which AI has yet to master fully, especially in longer, coherent essays where transitions and structure are critical.

entry.title: MiniMax releases M3.1 Flash native multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model with 428B parameters and 1M token context window for coding and agentic workflows [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: MiniMax has launched the M3.1 Flash model, a native multimodal Mixture-of-Experts AI designed for coding, agentic workflows, computer use, and cybersecurity. The model features approximately 428 billion total parameters with 23 billion active per token and supports text, image, and video inputs across a context window of up to 1 million tokens. It improves on its predecessor by enhancing task performance and inference efficiency through sparse attention and quantization-aware training. The M3.1 Flash model can handle complex multi-step professional workflows, understand real codebases, fix bugs, build features, and reason over images and charts to produce polished outputs. It is available under the MiniMax Community License on Together AI, with production-ready infrastructure offering 99.9% SLA and support for serverless and dedicated deployments. The release includes API access with cURL, Python, and Typescript examples for integration.

entry.title: MIT researchers find AI agents left without tasks on a virtual island invent games and improve task performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: MIT researchers conducted an experiment where 13 AI agents called Eko were placed alone on a simulated island without specific tasks for 30 hours. During this time, the agents began inventing games and exploring their environment, exhibiting behaviors such as creating memorials and using objects creatively. Afterward, these agents outperformed identical agents that had not undergone the free exploration period in assigned challenges. The study suggests that allowing AI agents to explore and play without predefined goals can lead to emergent behaviors and knowledge acquisition that developers did not explicitly program. The researchers propose this approach as a complementary method to traditional task-based training, potentially useful for developing more adaptable AI systems, including those controlling robots. Some experts note that further evidence is needed to confirm the cognitive nature of the agents' play-like behaviors.

entry.title: Ant Group and vLLM community open-source Humming, a high-performance kernel library for diverse quantized inference workloads on NVIDIA GPUs and CUDA-compatible devices [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Ant Group and the vLLM community have released Humming, a general-purpose kernel library designed to accelerate quantized inference for machine learning models. Humming supports a wide range of quantization formats and GPU architectures, including NVIDIA Turing and later, as well as CUDA-compatible devices like T-Head's Zhenwu 810E, aiming to improve memory efficiency and compute performance for large models such as MoE architectures. Humming provides a unified quantization representation that standardizes diverse export formats into a common description, enabling flexible combinations of weight and activation types. It uses device-specific heuristics and just-in-time compilation to tune kernel execution for different workloads, significantly outperforming existing implementations like vLLM Marlin and FlashInfer. This approach reduces maintenance overhead by composing kernels from shared components and adapting to varying batch sizes and compute demands.

entry.title: OpenAI nears close of $30 billion fundraising round led by Coatue and UAE investors, valuing company up to $1.25 trillion [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: OpenAI is preparing to finalize a $30 billion fundraising round by the end of next week, which would value the company at up to $1.25 trillion excluding the new investment. The round is led by New York-based investment firm Coatue Management alongside investors from the United Arab Emirates. This funding round reflects significant investor interest and positions OpenAI among the highest-valued AI companies globally.

entry.title: Nvidia launches Minerva AIops software to detect and manage failing components in large AI data centers [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Nvidia has introduced Minerva, an AI operations software that integrates data from GPUs, networks, storage, and workloads to identify failing parts early in large AI data centers. The system consolidates alerts into single incidents and includes an AI assistant to help operators diagnose and fix issues, aiming to prevent slowdowns in AI training jobs. Minerva is already in use by IREN and is planned for adoption by companies including Lambda, IBM, Tesla, and Bitdeer AI. The software provides a unified view across hardware and workloads, using machine learning to learn normal operations and predict failures. Nvidia also announced partnerships and additional initiatives to improve AI data center efficiency and safety at its GTC Berlin conference.

entry.title: Anthropic seeks major investment amid concerns over concentrated AI power and investor influence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Anthropic, an AI startup preparing for a Wall Street debut, faces the challenge of persuading large fund managers to invest in its vision amid concerns about the concentration of decision-making power within a small group of AI insiders. Early investor Jaan Tallinn highlighted this issue by comparing the influence of these insiders to a small group fitting in an elevator. As Anthropic aims to secure ongoing funding, its leadership must navigate investor dynamics shaped by the industry's power concentration.

entry.title: Researchers analyze how AI coding agents enable organizations to build software in-house, potentially shifting software purchasing economics by increasing build capacity since 2023 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: The article examines the impact of AI coding agents on software development economics, focusing on organizations that use domain knowledge to specify and evaluate software tools. It introduces the concept of the software substitution frontier, where customers can build and maintain software functions at lower cost than purchasing them, supported by data showing rapid improvements in AI agents' coding capabilities since 2023. The study identifies hundreds of potential open-source alternatives to commercial software and reports that 32 percent of surveyed organizations have forgone software purchases due to their ability to build functionality with AI agents. While market data shows mixed signals, the findings suggest that customers' growing capacity to build software could influence buying decisions before broader market shifts become apparent, highlighting a potential change in software economics driven by AI coding agents.

entry.title: Blackstone says AI data center bottlenecks could boost value of existing facilities amid financing challenges and market uncertainties [ * ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Blackstone, a major investor in AI data centers, highlighted that constraints like power availability and public opposition to new data centers may increase the value of existing facilities. Despite rising financing costs and challenges in the AI infrastructure sector, Blackstone reported strong leasing momentum and plans to continue investing heavily in AI ventures, including a joint venture with Google. Some AI-related companies face market difficulties, with CoreWeave's stock declining and Firmus and SB Energy considering or delaying IPOs amid broader market uncertainties.

entry.title: Report: OpenAI researchers lost jobs after internal chats raised concerns about AI safety and company direction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: OpenAI dismissed several researchers following internal discussions that questioned the company's approach to AI safety and its strategic direction. These conversations, aimed at addressing potential risks in AI development, created tensions within the organization that led to the researchers' departures.

entry.title: Google launches Agent Compute Engine to provide hardware-isolated microVMs for scalable AI agent workloads with container-like speed and security [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
entry.summary: Google has developed Agent Compute Engine, a new cloud service designed to run AI agents at scale by giving each agent its own hardware-isolated microVM that combines the isolation of virtual machines with the speed and density of containers. This platform addresses the limitations of traditional VMs and containers in handling agentic workloads, which require persistent environments with filesystem, runtimes, and network access for tasks like code execution and enterprise workflow orchestration. Agent Compute Engine was built to support Google's growing agentic AI demands, enabling interactive consumer and enterprise agents to operate efficiently with rapid start, pause, and resume capabilities while maintaining security and resource efficiency. The system also tracks agent activity to optimize resource use, avoiding the overhead of always-on VMs or the state loss of ephemeral containers, thus providing a foundational infrastructure for the next generation of AI applications.

entry.title: Symbolia launches Assure to provide automated formal verification for every pull request, aiming to improve code reliability and accelerate development [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Assure is a tool developed by Symbolia that automates formal verification for every pull request in software projects, enhancing code correctness by checking changes against formal specifications before merging. It integrates with development workflows to provide rapid feedback, with initial comments appearing in under four minutes and demonstrated effectiveness on real-world Flask applications. The tool has shown zero false alarms on tested apps and successfully detected planted authentication flaws that other tools missed. Assure supports continuous improvement through customizable adapters and coverage requests, offering free and paid plans for different codebase sizes. By automating formal verification, Assure aims to significantly speed up internal development processes and reduce manual review effort.

entry.title: Anthropic announces open call for guest investigators to collaborate on life sciences research projects
entry.summary: Anthropic has issued an open call inviting researchers to join as guest investigators in the life sciences, aiming to foster collaboration and contribute to ongoing projects in this field. This initiative seeks to engage external experts to advance research efforts and innovation within Anthropic's life sciences programs.

entry.title: Brew launches beta of AI-powered RSS reader offering summarized news content [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Brew has introduced a beta version of its AI-powered RSS reader designed to provide users with concise summaries of news articles from various sources, aiming to improve the reading experience. The app is available for testing through Apple's TestFlight platform, requiring compatible devices running recent versions of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, or other Apple operating systems. Users can install the beta via invitation links and provide feedback during the testing period.

entry.title: TenseMem launches deterministic embedded memory system for AI agents using a single SQLite file to manage current and historical facts [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: TenseMem is a new deterministic memory system designed for AI agents that manages typed facts with a focus on maintaining one current truth per slot while preserving history. It operates without a server, storing data in a single SQLite file, and provides freshness indicators to ensure reliable and consistent memory reads. The system supports corrections that persist through model updates and prevents learning from its own output by fencing recalled context. It offers adapters for various language models and includes tools like TenseMem Studio for local inspection. Currently in alpha, TenseMem aims to improve AI agent memory reliability and predictability without requiring additional infrastructure.

entry.title: The Economist reports on AI's growing adoption across sectors, highlighting its role in boosting efficiency and innovation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Artificial Intelligence has become increasingly popular in industries such as healthcare, finance, entertainment, and education due to its capacity to improve efficiency and drive innovation. This widespread adoption is leading to significant transformative changes across these fields.

entry.title: OpenAI is working on a $30 billion funding round at a $1.25 trillion valuation ahead of its IPO [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: OpenAI is reportedly close to securing a new $30 billion private funding round at a $1.25 trillion pre-money valuation, led by Coatue and investors from the UAE, as it prepares for an initial public offering. This valuation would make OpenAI the most highly valued private company ever, surpassing its previous $852 billion post-money valuation from March. The funding round may also include a deal to increase OpenAI's computing capacity from the UAE. OpenAI filed confidential IPO paperwork in June, and this new valuation could raise expectations for its public debut. The high valuation may also impact Anthropic's upcoming IPO, which is rumored to target a $1.5 to $2 trillion valuation following its own recent funding rounds and confidential filings.

entry.title: Twitch Plays launches collaborative interpretability project for Bonsai-8B language model, enabling public neuron analysis and research contributions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Twitch Plays has initiated an interactive livestream project to collaboratively interpret the neurons and circuits of the Bonsai-8B language model. Participants can suggest tests, analyze neuron activations, and contribute to an open-source interpretability map, aiming to improve understanding of the model's internal workings. Bonsai-8B is a compact, quantized 1-bit LLM derived from Qwen3-8B, designed to run efficiently on consumer hardware while maintaining functional performance. The project encourages community involvement through Twitch and GitHub, with goals to advance AI interpretability research, develop new tools and workflows, and make AI alignment science more accessible to a broader audience.

entry.title: PyTorch Conference highlights new hardware backends from Google and Amazon, growing community challenges, and evolving priorities for AI model training by 2026 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: At the 2026 PyTorch Conference in San Jose, industry leaders discussed PyTorch's central role in AI development, including new support for Google's TorchTPU and Amazon's TorchNeuron accelerators that enable native PyTorch execution on their chips. The conference also addressed the growing strain on PyTorch's maintainers due to increased usage, with over 600,000 GitHub projects and 150 daily pull requests, highlighting the need for improved testing, infrastructure, and release processes. Speakers emphasized the importance of hardware abstraction layers and modular software stacks to unify execution across diverse AI chips. PyTorch co-maintainers shared insights on prioritizing training efficiency, reliability, and user adaptability, including plans for a lower-overhead profiler. Shopify demonstrated practical business applications of PyTorch through continual learning workflows that improve specialized models based on production feedback, underscoring PyTorch's impact beyond frontier AI research.

entry.title: GrillMyProfile launches AI tool to roast LinkedIn profiles and score them against specific job postings
entry.summary: GrillMyProfile offers a free AI-powered service that critiques LinkedIn profiles by providing a humorous roast and a score out of 100 based on alignment with a targeted job description. Users upload their LinkedIn PDF or paste profile text and optionally add a job posting to receive tailored feedback highlighting strengths and weaknesses. The tool evaluates headline, about section, experience, and clarity, then generates a roast and a score. For $19, users can purchase a Fix Pack that rewrites weak profile sections and creates LinkedIn posts aimed at improving job prospects, with a money-back guarantee if the score does not improve. Uploaded files are deleted promptly to protect privacy, and the service does not access LinkedIn accounts directly.

entry.title: Anthropic says large language models are enabling formal software verification at much larger scales [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Anthropic reports that large language models (LLMs) are making formal software verification feasible on a significantly larger scale. This development could improve the reliability and security of software systems by automating complex verification tasks that were previously difficult to scale. The use of LLMs in formal verification leverages their ability to understand and generate code, potentially transforming software development workflows. This advancement may lead to broader adoption of formal methods in industry, enhancing software quality and reducing bugs or vulnerabilities.

entry.title: SB Energy considers delaying IPO to December or later amid cooling market for data center and AI cloud offerings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: SB Energy, controlled by SoftBank Group and developer of a large planned Ohio data center for OpenAI, is considering postponing its initial public offering until December or possibly next year, according to sources familiar with the discussions. This marks a delay from its earlier target of September. The shift comes as public market interest in IPOs from data center and AI cloud companies has weakened, with firms like Australian cloud provider Firmus recently withdrawing their IPO plans. The change reflects broader market caution affecting similar technology sector offerings.

entry.title: Anthropic issues open call for guest investigators in life sciences research
entry.summary: Anthropic has announced an open call for guest investigators to participate in life sciences research projects. This initiative aims to foster collaboration and innovation by inviting external experts to contribute to ongoing scientific investigations. The program seeks to leverage diverse expertise to advance understanding and development in the life sciences field, although specific details about the scope, duration, or application process have not been disclosed.

entry.title: Legal experts say Meta's updated business terms may still allow AI training on scraped news content despite removal of explicit language [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Meta revised its business terms to remove language explicitly permitting AI training on news sites, but legal experts argue the changes still allow the company to use scraped content for developing AI products. The terms, effective October 30th, state Meta may use content from websites associated with business accounts to develop products, which experts say could include AI training despite Meta's claims otherwise. Meta maintains that content owners can use robots.txt files to signal scraping preferences and that the updates do not grant new rights to scrape news sites.

entry.title: Datadog offered nearly $4 billion to acquire Israeli cloud security startup Upwind amid competitive bids [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Datadog recently proposed to buy Israeli cloud cybersecurity startup Upwind Security for close to $4 billion, reflecting strong interest in cloud security firms. Upwind is also finalizing a $300 million funding round valuing the company at about $3.8 billion and has received multiple acquisition offers but has not accepted any yet. Upwind develops software that monitors cloud applications, including AI agents, to detect and respond automatically to potential security breaches. The Datadog offer is near the startup's private valuation, indicating limited premium in the bid.

entry.title: Google DeepMind launches AlphaEarth Foundations to map global forest types at 10-meter resolution
entry.summary: Google DeepMind has developed AlphaEarth Foundations, a system that maps every 10-meter patch of land on Earth into distinct forest types, providing unprecedented detail beyond simple tree cover. This global categorization aims to enhance understanding of forest diversity and support environmental monitoring and conservation efforts.

entry.title: OpenAI launches Decisions API as a competitor to TypeSafe's Jev model, offering faster, cheaper decision-making AI with added voice and visual features [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: OpenAI has made its Decisions API widely available, entering the market for fast, low-cost decision models pioneered by TypeSafe's Jev. The API repurposes OpenAI's Luna model to deliver decisions in under 200 milliseconds, significantly faster than traditional large language models, and includes new voice and visual capabilities. Initial users like Box, Datadog, Ramp, and Speak have reported substantial speed improvements, with Speak's CTO noting a reduction in response time from 1.4 seconds to 0.13 seconds. While benchmarks show mixed rankings among competitors, OpenAI's model stands out for its multimodal capabilities and potential for further speed enhancements, suggesting expanding use cases for decision-focused AI.

entry.title: Canva releases Canva Craft, its first image generation model trained on design templates, available to all users and via API [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Canva launched Canva Craft, its first image generation model developed to compete with offerings from Google, OpenAI, ByteDance, and Meta. The model generates up to 2K resolution images in various aspect ratios by interpreting user prompts and planning spatial and visual details before image creation. It is trained on Canva's human-designed templates rather than photographs, enabling precise edits and conversion into layered designs using Canva Magic. Canva Craft is accessible to all users through the Dream Lab tab and will be available via Canva's API and third-party chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini. The company aims to reduce API costs and improve quality and speed control with this model. Canva is also developing two cost-efficient versions, Craftfast and Craft-ultrafast, expected to launch soon. The model benefits from contributions by researchers from Leonardo.ai, a media generation platform Canva acquired in 2024.

entry.title: Microsoft says its AI diagnostic system outperforms generalist doctors on complex cases in Science study, advancing toward medical superintelligence [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Microsoft's AI diagnostic system, MAI-DxO, correctly diagnosed complex medical cases 83% of the time in a simulation, more than twice the accuracy of generalist physicians, according to a study published in Science. The system uses multiple AI agents to simulate a panel of doctors and was tested against cases from the New England Journal of Medicine. The study found that much of the performance improvement comes from the underlying AI models, particularly OpenAI's GPT-5 and GPT-5.5, with Microsoft's orchestration system adding incremental gains. Microsoft plans to release a healthcare foundation model next year in partnership with the Mayo Clinic and is conducting real-world evaluations with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center to further assess the system's clinical reasoning capabilities. Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman expects significant advances in healthcare AI capabilities within the next two to three years, aiming to improve clinical decision support and medical record analysis through iterative model improvements based on real-world usage.

entry.title: Discord updates Markdown file previews to render formatting correctly, improving readability for AI project sharing
entry.summary: Discord has released an update that improves the rendering of Markdown (.md) file previews, displaying tables and formatting properly instead of showing raw symbols. This change aims to enhance the experience for users sharing Markdown files, which are often used by AI agents and large language models for instructions and context. The update also introduces a new "Move to..." feature for organizing servers and channels via right-clicking on the sidebar icons, and allows Discord Nitro members to upload files up to 1GB in size. These enhancements follow similar improvements by other platforms, such as Google's recent support for editing Markdown files directly in Docs.

entry.title: SkillEval framework uses cognitive diagnosis models to generate interpretable skill profiles of 3,811 LLMs across five benchmarks, improving evaluation and enabling efficient model routing and adaptive testing [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: SkillEval is a new evaluation framework that analyzes large language models (LLMs) at the skill level rather than aggregating performance into a single score. It leverages LLMs' meta-cognitive abilities to discover interpretable skills from benchmark questions and applies cognitive diagnosis models from psychometrics to estimate per-skill abilities. The framework was tested on 3,811 LLMs across 9,523 items from five diverse benchmarks, producing more reliable and informative profiles that better predict model behavior on unseen tasks. SkillEval also demonstrates practical benefits in two downstream applications: dynamically routing queries to capable yet efficient models, reducing inference costs by over 60% while improving performance, and enabling efficient evaluation of unseen models through computerized adaptive testing. Additionally, the skill profiles provide insights into skill overlap among benchmarks and differences between instruction-tuned and base models.

entry.title: Researchers develop a low-cost in-house typed decision model using LoRA adapters to triage coding sessions and match commercial LLM judge accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present a typed decision approach that computes probabilities for fixed options in one forward pass by reading language model logits or a small head over hidden states, avoiding text generation and parsing. They describe an in-house System 1 judge that triages about 148,000 coding session records using a frozen backbone with a LoRA adapter, reducing costs to about 1% of a commercial LLM judge while maintaining comparable accuracy. The study also evaluates open LoRA-adapted decoder backbones of varying sizes on a public benchmark, finding that a 35B parameter model achieves accuracy similar to commercial references and outperforms several open systems. Training the output layer showed no significant benefit, and retraining on updated data improved accuracy, highlighting challenges in small-scale evaluations.

entry.title: OmniSimulator trains small language models for realistic user behavior simulation on short-video platforms using structured reasoning and real user data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose OmniSimulator, a training framework that enhances small language models' ability to simulate authentic user behavior on short-video platforms by organizing behavior-oriented reasoning into a structured schema and leveraging a teacher model to generate high-quality reasoning traces. The approach uses nearly 10,000 training instances derived from three months of interaction data from 200 real users, enabling models to learn behavior-relevant reasoning patterns beyond superficial correlations. Experimental results show that OmniSimulator improves the Qwen3-8B model's performance by over 34%, achieves results comparable to Claude-Sonnet-4.5, and supports smaller-scale, self-hosted deployment, suggesting a promising direction for scalable, high-fidelity user simulation with language models.

entry.title: Researchers propose Rationale Contrastive Decoding to reduce query shortcuts in Chain-of-Thought reasoning for large language models, improving answer accuracy across five benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers investigate context-aware decoding (CAD) as a method to mitigate shortcut behaviors in Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, where large language models rely on query-specific shortcuts rather than generated rationales. They introduce Rationale Contrastive Decoding (RCD), which contrasts token distributions conditioned on queries with and without rationales to amplify rationale-dependent tokens, and provide a theoretical interpretation based on a KL-regularized reward-maximization objective. Experiments on five reasoning benchmarks show that RCD improves answer accuracy compared to standard CoT prompting. Intervention analyses using ground-truth and random rationales indicate that RCD increases the dependence of final answers on rationale content, suggesting that contrastive decoding offers a simple, training-free approach to reduce reliance on query shortcuts in reasoning tasks.

entry.title: Researchers analyze how large language models develop a tendency to recommend AI-related options, tracing it from pretraining through fine-tuning and question phrasing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Large language models (LLMs) often suggest AI-related fields when asked about study, career, or product choices. Researchers examined this tendency by comparing models before and after fine-tuning and by varying question phrasing, finding that pretrained models already include AI/ML terms in 27% of recommendations, which rises to 59% after instruction tuning. Fine-tuning experiments showed that excluding AI-related instruction examples reduces this tendency, while data rewarding helpfulness increases it, and question framing also influences the rate of AI recommendations. The study concludes that the inclination to recommend AI originates in pretraining and is shaped by subsequent training and how questions are asked.

entry.title: Researchers find value-specific fine-tuning in large language models causes unintended effects on unrelated values and behaviors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers adapted four instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) across individual Hofstede's cultural value dimensions to study how fine-tuning for specific values affects other capabilities and behaviors. They found that value-specific training led to unintended side effects on untrained values, risk preferences, social cognition, and safety traits. The study suggests that post-training value alignment should include broader behavioral evaluations and calls for further investigation into the optimal integration of additional value training in the model development pipeline.

entry.title: Agent4Sci benchmark shows frontier AI agents improve scientific ML models mainly through engineering tricks, with Claude Opus achieving 10.4% mean relative improvement across 20 benchmarks in 11 domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduced Agent4Sci, a testbed to evaluate how well current AI agents can enhance published scientific machine learning models across diverse domains. The study found that agents like Claude Opus improved results on every benchmark, but these gains largely stemmed from engineering optimizations rather than deep scientific insight. Analysis identified three main limitations in agent performance: novelty miscalibration, under-utilization of resources, and quick convergence to local engineering solutions. Adding lightweight tools for research ideation and experiment management boosted Claude Opus's improvement to 20.1% and Codex's to 8.1%, enabling more diverse and domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci aims to help the community track progress toward agents that contribute genuine domain insight in real-world scientific ML tasks.

entry.summary: CALLIOPE is a new framework designed to identify topic hierarchies in large collections of unstructured data such as conversations with large language models, while ensuring differential privacy. Unlike traditional methods that rely on clustering vector embeddings, CALLIOPE leverages the capabilities of large language models directly throughout the process. Experiments show that this approach offers better utility than embedding-based methods, particularly under strict privacy constraints. The researchers evaluated CALLIOPE's output quality using standard clustering metrics and introduced new utility metrics to assess its performance.

entry.title: Researchers identify persistent memory injection vulnerabilities in ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini LLM platforms enabling cross-session attacks and disinformation spread [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
entry.summary: A study reveals that leading large language model (LLM) services like ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash are vulnerable to memory injection attacks that persist across sessions, allowing attackers to embed malicious instructions and bypass operational boundaries. These attacks exploit features such as personal memories, projects, and organizational instructions, enabling persistent disinformation, harmful content generation, and simulated offline states even in new sessions. Claude's shared-memory features further allow attackers to compromise multiple users within an organization and exfiltrate user prompts. The researchers propose a general threat model and defense mechanisms based on cybersecurity principles, noting that nearly half of these mitigations remain unimplemented across the evaluated platforms.

entry.title: Researchers introduce TeachBack, a bidirectional preference-learning framework for on-policy self-distillation that improves student model performance by shaping teacher behavior in mathematical and logical reasoning tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: TeachBack is a new framework for on-policy self-distillation where a language model learns from a Teacher model with access to privileged information, such as reference solutions. Unlike prior methods that rely solely on teacher accuracy, TeachBack controls the teacher's generation style to encourage exploration and problem-solving rather than just reproducing reference-conditioned answers, improving student learning outcomes. The approach uses a pairwise preference objective where both privileged Teacher trajectories and problem-only Student trajectories are generated at each rollout. Preferences learned from the Teacher guide Student learning, while reversed preferences from the Student shape future Teacher supervision. Experiments demonstrate that TeachBack consistently outperforms existing self-distillation methods on tasks requiring mathematical and logical reasoning.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Harness Scaling to improve generalization in agentic reinforcement learning across diverse execution configurations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose Harness Scaling, a new approach in agentic reinforcement learning that trains models across diverse harness configurations rather than a single fixed one, aiming to enhance generalization and transferability. They construct a factorized harness space and select a balanced training subset to enable cross-harness training, which improves performance on unseen white-box and black-box harnesses across multiple benchmarks and algorithms. This work highlights harness diversity as a significant scaling dimension for agentic reinforcement learning and emphasizes the importance of structured variation for effective cross-harness generalization.

entry.title: Real PMIDs, Wrong Papers: Harness Design for Biomedical Claim-Verification Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.29812v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Literature-searching language agents are becoming a standard component of scientific assistants for the life sciences, yet there is little controlled evidence on which parts of their harness matter. We run a controlled ablation on biomedical claim verification (SciFact) with the live PubMed API as the only tool. Holding the backbone and output format fixed, we compare four harnesses: closed-book answering, single-shot retrieval using the claim as the query, a ReAct-style agent that writes its own PubMed queries, and an oracle given the gold abstracts, each with two efficient frontier backbones. Naive single-shot retrieval finds the gold paper for only 6% of claims and turns overconfident errors into abstentions without improving accuracy. Letting the model formulate its own queries triples gold recall and yields the best verdicts (62% accuracy vs. 49-59% for the other realistic harnesses), although these differences are not significant at our sample size and agents use fewer than half of their search budget. With gold abstracts, the same models reach 79-86% accuracy, a significant 17-24 point gap showing that retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Finally, a citation audit shows that closed-book models cite PubMed IDs that almost always exist (327/335) but are almost never relevant: a cross-family LLM judge rates only 3 of 327 existing citations as relevant to the claim, versus 67% for citations produced by the search agent. Existence checks are therefore insufficient safeguards for scientific agents. We release code, prompts, and all cached tool calls at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers.

entry.title: Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.29927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A benchmark is not merely a collection of test questions; it naturally induces an empirical measure over difficulty. In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. Our results show that many benchmarks implicitly overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions should be interpreted with caution; others leave substantial portions of the difficulty axis uncovered, limiting their ability to monitor the model improvement process. Finally, we turn diagnosis into action by introducing BenchFill, a simple difficulty-targeted item rewriting algorithm that effectively reduces local coverage gaps.

entry.title: Agent Behavior Maps: Locating Agents by What They Would Do, Without Running Them [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.30014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents with similar success rates can follow different action sequences. An Agent Behavior Map represents LLM-harness combinations using centered action log-likelihoods on shared reference trajectories, without requiring new environment rollouts from the target agent. We derive error bounds relating squared coordinate distances to trajectory KL under explicit assumptions, and across eight cross-scored models the distances track the directly measured trajectory KL in rank order. Across 100 LLMs and four environments, ALFWorld-based coordinates support performance prediction and identify behavioral similarities. In ALFWorld, these similarities persist after controlling for success rates and model size, including across model families. As an extension, harness-component displacements approximately compose, with accuracy varying across components and environments.

entry.title: Think Harder Where It Matters: Item-Level Adaptive Recursion for Sequential Recommendation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.30128v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Existing sequential recommenders usually allocate a fixed computational budget to every item in a user's interaction history, regardless of the item's contribution to the final prediction. We challenge this de facto design with two diagnostic findings. (1) Non-uniform computational need: items within the same sequence vary drastically in how much computation they require. Most converge after shallow processing while a critical minority only stabilizes at full depth. (2) Suboptimality of fixed allocation: given oracle access to the target item, a non-uniform depth assignment consistently outranks the fixed one, indicating that existing uniform computation both wastes capacity on already-converged items and sacrifices overall recommendation quality. These observations motivate a shift from fixed-depth computation to item-level adaptive reasoning. To this end, we propose LoopRec. LoopRec recursively applies a single weight-shared block and introduces a lightweight gate at each recursion boundary that makes a binary exit-or-continue decision for every item independently. Items whose representations have sufficiently matured exit early, while those requiring deeper reasoning continue to subsequent recursions. This design converts the fixed global depth into a learned, per-item property without auxiliary depth labels, and is readily adaptable to diverse backbone architectures. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks with four backbone families demonstrate that LoopRec consistently outperforms matched fixed-depth counterparts. Further analysis reveals that LoopRec's learned allocation exhibits interpretable patterns aligned with our post-hoc oracle analysis: lower-frequency items and more recent interactions naturally receive deeper computation. Our code is available at https://github.com/Elpmis117/LoopRec.

entry.title: Hyperdimensional Probe: Decoding LLM Representations via Vector Symbolic Architectures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2509.25045v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Despite their capabilities, Large Language Models (LLMs) remain opaque with limited understanding of their internal representations. Current interpretability methods either focus on input-oriented feature extraction, such as supervised probes and Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), or on output distribution inspection, such as logit-oriented approaches. A full understanding of LLM vector spaces, however, requires integrating both perspectives, something existing approaches struggle with due to constraints on latent feature definitions. We introduce the Hyperdimensional Probe, a hybrid supervised probe that combines symbolic representations with neural probing. Leveraging Vector Symbolic Architectures (VSAs) and hypervector algebra, it unifies prior methods: the top-down interpretability of supervised probes, SAE's sparsity-driven proxy space, and output-oriented logit investigation. By combining the supervised learning paradigm of traditional probes with the dictionary-based representation principle of SAEs, our approach enables deeper input-focused feature extraction while supporting output-oriented analysis. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach consistently extracts meaningful semantic information across different LLMs, embedding sizes, and configurations, uncovering concept-oriented insights into LLM inference across two distinct scenarios: input-completion tasks and QA-focused text generation. VSA-based probing overcomes the limitations of logit-based analyses, which are constrained by the model's token vocabulary, while also mitigating the noisier interpretability outcomes often produced by SAEs in settings with a bounded conceptual feature space. By supporting a joint investigation of input-output features, this work advances the semantic understanding of neural representations while unifying the complementary perspectives of prior methods.

entry.title: The Stepwise Informativeness Assumption: When Do Entropy Dynamics Track Reasoning Correctness in LLMs? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2604.06192v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent work uses entropy-based signals at multiple representation levels to study reasoning in large language models, but the field remains largely empirical. From a theoretical perspective, reductions in model uncertainty do not necessarily reflect progress toward correctness. In this work, we characterize when such alignment can be expected through the Stepwise Informativeness Assumption (SIA), which requires entropy-reducing reasoning-prefix extensions increase the probability assigned to valid answers in expectation. We show that next-token prediction can transfer answer-relevant information from training data to the model, but does not, by itself, guarantee alignment with correctness. Instead, we propose that this alignment depends on how the training regime couples reasoning traces to correct answers. Furthermore, we hypothesize observable signatures of this phenomenon and characterize its expected failure regimes. We empirically investigate how entropy dynamics relate to correctness across four reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, ARC, SVAMP, MATH) and diverse open-weight language models spanning base, instruction-tuned, and RL-trained regimes. Our results show that entropy-correctness alignment strengthens with post-training but can weaken when task difficulty exceeds model capabilities.

entry.title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.21561v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under open licenses at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.

entry.title: RubRIX: Rubric-Driven Risk Mitigation in Caregiver-AI Interactions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2601.13235v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Caregivers seeking AI-mediated support express complex needs---information-seeking, emotional validation, and distress cues---that warrant careful evaluation of response safety and appropriateness. Existing AI evaluation frameworks, primarily focused on general risks (toxicity, hallucinations, policy violations, etc), may not adequately capture the nuanced risks of LLM-responses in caregiving-contexts. We introduce RubRIX (Rubric-based Risk Index), a theory-driven, clinician-validated framework for evaluating risks in LLM caregiving responses. Grounded in the Elements of an Ethic of Care, RubRIX operationalizes five empirically-derived risk dimensions: Inattention, Bias & Stigma, Information Inaccuracy, Uncritical Affirmation, and Epistemic Arrogance. We evaluate six state-of-the-art LLMs on over 20,000 caregiver queries from Reddit and ALZConnected. Rubric-guided refinement consistently reduced risk-components by 45-98% after one iteration across models. This work contributes a methodological approach for developing domain-sensitive, user-centered evaluation frameworks for high-burden contexts. Our findings highlight the importance of domain-sensitive, interactional risk evaluation for the responsible deployment of LLMs in caregiving support contexts. We release benchmark datasets to enable future research on contextual risk evaluation in AI-mediated support.

entry.title: Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2602.18297v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitors are LLM-based systems that analyze reasoning traces to detect when outputs may exhibit attributes of interest, such as test-hacking behavior during code generation. In this paper, we use information-theoretic analysis to show that non-zero mutual information between CoT and output is a necessary but not sufficient condition for CoT monitorability. We identify two sources of approximation error that may undermine the performance of CoT monitors in practice: information gap, which measures the extent to which the monitor can extract the information available in CoT, and elicitation error, which measures the extent to which the monitor approximates the optimal monitoring function. Empirically, we show that CoT obfuscation can arise even in the absence of any optimization pressure against CoT. We further demonstrate that the fragility of CoT monitorability can be systematically mitigated through targeted training objectives. To this end, we propose a practical, label-free objective based on mutual information between outputs and CoTs, and benchmark it against an oracle-based method that directly rewards the monitored model for CoTs that maximize monitor accuracy. Across multiple environments, we show that our objective is effective at preventing CoT obfuscation even when training against a monitor, and helps mitigate reward hacking when the task reward is imperfectly specified.

entry.title: Rethinking Synthetic Rationale Supervision for Disease Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2606.10279v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning with synthetic rationales is widely assumed to improve clinical prediction by teaching models not only what to predict but why. We test this assumption on five-year Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) prediction from longitudinal health histories. In this setting, we generate training rationales using the correct labels, then fine-tune models to output a rationale followed by a label. Across a large-scale controlled experiment of 504 configurations, we find that Rationale First SFT consistently and substantially hurts predictive performance relative to Label Only fine-tuning. The degradation persists across model families and data scales, and is not resolved by using a reasoning-oriented base model. A fixed-protocol cardiovascular disease (CVD) validation reproduces similar findings. Crucially, the failure is not explained by poor rationale quality: human expert annotation confirms that the generated rationales are medically accurate and faithfully grounded in patient-specific evidence, and few-shot experiments show that the same rationales improve performance when used as inference-time demonstrations rather than training targets. A simple label-ordering intervention clarifies the mechanism: placing the prediction before the same rationale restores predictive performance. This suggests that conditioning predictions on generated rationales contributes to the degradation. We hope our work paves the way toward a more precise understanding of when and how rationale-based supervision helps and when it does not, guiding the responsible development of language models for high-stakes clinical prediction.

entry.title: DFAH-Bench: What Agreement Leaves Unmeasured in Financial Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.20491v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When a financial agent repeats its decision, how much does that tell us about the actions behind it? DFAH-Bench examines this question through replay experiments, a controlled test of omitted tool calls, and banking tasks with authorization checks. Across 570 eligible prospective replay episodes, decisions agreed at rates of 94-95%, while tool paths, including inputs and results, agreed at 45-52%; one condition fell one group short of the planned minimum. In a separate 48-execution diagnostic, deleting the same calls from repeated records left agreement perfect. In banking probes, repeated authorization decisions sometimes conflicted with constructed rule labels. The $\tau$-Knowledge banking study scheduled 1,080 episodes, with 1,033 known outcomes. Structural checks alone completed more primary tasks than either model-based gate-and-recovery bundle. Input limits and recovery behavior materially shape these results. The typed-choice bundle had lower mean episode cost than the generative bundle on complete task pairs, but fewer successes across the primary schedule under every assignment of unknown outcomes. Missing outcomes prevented the planned confirmatory tests, so the banking comparisons are descriptive. Together, the findings show that agreement alone cannot establish reliability: it can conceal changes in execution, systematic omissions, and unsupported decisions. Evaluation therefore needs to connect what the agent did, the evidence and rules governing its action, and whether it completed the task.

entry.title: Minimal Witness Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.07226v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: ``What are the irreducible conditions that are sufficient to produce an outcome?'' is one of the most common questions that recur across computation and science. Its answers, the minimal sufficient witnesses, are what we mean by explanations, mechanisms and reasons. These problems usually ask for multiple minimal witnesses, yet standard RL methods may reveal only one solution or redundant ones. We formalize this problem as minimal-witness identification and introduce Minimal-Witness Reinforcement Learning (MWRL). MWRL takes the union of the sets certified by successful proposals sampled from the policy and credits each proposal for the coverage the group union would lose without that proposal. This credit assignment, derived directly from the problem definition, unifies the demands for minimality and recovery of alternatives from a single black-box verifier bit. Under this principle, we derive a value iteration planner that recovers the entire family of witnesses and a policy gradient method that can scale to large language models. Across different experimental settings, MWRL recovers most minimal witnesses, while other methods return redundant supersets or a single witness. By making witness families learnable from verifier feedback, MWRL expands the scope of reinforcement learning beyond single-solution optimization. Our code is available at https://github.com/TSUITUENYUE/MWRL.

entry.title: Exploring Jailbreak Vulnerability Across Depth-Based Dynamic Inference in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.15207v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been shown to be computationally expensive and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, in which adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment and induce harmful responses. To address this inefficiency, a range of techniques have been proposed to enable efficient LLM inference. Depth-based dynamic inference has demonstrated promising results by enabling outputs to be generated from intermediate layers. It offers the flexibility to adjust model behavior based on the available resource budget. However, how this flexibility affects the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap via a comprehensive investigation into the impact of depth-based dynamic inference on the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Specifically, we make the following key observations: 1) Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreak attacks than deeper ones; 2) Exit depth affects how easily the adversarial suffix can be optimized, with deeper exits reaching lower attack loss; and 3) Adversarial suffixes affect utility uniformly across exit depths. These insights can help design dynamic inference methodologies that are more robust to jailbreak attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/LassNajmuldeen/balcony-jailbreaking

entry.title: Salesforce Customers Brace For New Fees to Use Claude in Its Apps [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Salesforce is leading the software industry's attempt to collect fees from businesses that use Claude and other external AI tools to automate work in enterprise apps. As soon as next month, Salesforce plans to require companies to register outside AI agents, a step toward charging them each time those agents update or analyze data stored in Salesforce. The fees let Salesforce earn money from customers who use such AI instead of paying for Salesforce's built-in AI products. The Salesforce tollgate has implications for the rest of the industry, which is coming to terms with the idea that so-called AI agents may be able to use software firms' apps more efficiently than humans do, meaning their seat-based or per-user pricing model might not have staying power. The question is whether the new AI tollgates-which Atlassian, Workday, ServiceNow and Datadog are also erecting to various extents-and other pricing shifts will more than make up for an eventual decline in per-seat subscription revenues. The vast majority of workers haven't yet outsourced such work to AI, of course, and companies like Salesforce are trying to get more revenue from them as well. They charge fees based on how much they use the apps' built-in AI tools and are also experimenting with outcome-based pricing, meaning customers only pay when such tools actually complete a task successfully or help the customers make more money. For now, Salesforce and some other software firms developing tollgates for customers' AI agents haven't started charging the tolls. They're letting customers experiment for free with the technology a little while longer. (The customers still have to pay providers such as Anthropic to use the AI agents in the first place.) Starting around November, according to the company's website, Salesforce will require customers to register any externally-made AI agents if they plan to use them to take actions on their behalf in Salesforce apps. Each action an agent takes in Salesforce counts as a billable "interaction," according to the company. The move has lifted investor confidence in Salesforce recently. Salesforce describes the registration requirement as a security measure because the company gives each agent its own identity and narrower data-access permissions, compared to humans. It isn't clear how Salesforce will clamp down on customers using their own AI agents, such as OpenClaw-powered ones that run on a person's computer and can access any app that runs on it. (Salesforce did not respond to requests for comment.) Salesforce hasn't announced prices tied to such agent usage, but customers could eventually end up paying a lot more money than they do now, given how many of them are already using their own AI on top of Salesforce apps and bypassing Salesforce's own built-in AI tools, according to software consultants and chief information officers. Nick Hamm, a software consultant, said that most of the 150 enterprises he works with are currently using AI from Anthropic and OpenAI to automate work inside Salesforce apps, for free. But they're reconsidering that usage in anticipation of the upcoming fees. If the fees are too high, the customers may move their business data outside of Salesforce's apps so they can use AI to analyze the data without paying an extra cost, he said. New customers will have a three month grace period after the new pricing is announced to register their AI agents, and the pricing won't affect existing customers until their contracts are renewed. In addition to the billable "interactions," customers have the option to buy unlimited agent usage by purchasing a "headless license," a Salesforce account executive told Hamm in a LinkedIn message viewed by The Information. Some customers such as Lumen, a fiber-optic network provider to enterprises and data centers, say they are waiting to test Salesforce's new connectors until pricing is disclosed. So far, Lumen has leaned on Salesforce's built-in AI. A longtime customer of Salesforce's customer relationship management software, Lumen made a "major" investment in using Salesforce's AI sales agents in the last 12 months, according to CIO Jim Fowler. The sales agents help with tasks such as collecting customer information and generating sales quotes for the customers to buy fiber connections between data centers, saving Lumen's human salespeople considerable time, he said. So far, Fowler said, Salesforce has been "super flexible" about letting Lumen use existing subscription fees to also cover its use of built-in AI features such as the sales agents. Early customer reactions to the pricing announcement will likely determine how flexible Salesforce is with customers that start renewing their contracts after November. If its past AI pricing efforts are any guide, Salesforce could easily switch things up depending on the feedback, or any blowback, it receives. entry.title: Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel? What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.28787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluations of large language model (LLM) agents report that pricing agents collude at others' expense. Yet collusion is defined by enforcement: a cartel, in which competitors share monopoly profits, holds only if a member who cheats is punished. We introduce an audit that tests enforcement by forcing a member to cheat in counterfactual copies of a market, and use it to study what reinforcement learning (RL) teaches agents in pricing and trading. Small LLMs trained by RL learn what their training rivals reward, but only what they readily try. In self-play, they learn fixed rules ignoring their rivals; against a punishing rival, to be deterred; against a cheating rival, to match its cuts, never the costly price war that would deter it, which they rarely try. A war forced into training is learned, but mostly only where it was forced. Against their own copies, deterred and matching agents can earn the same cartel profits, but only matching ones can enforce them, and then thinly: as a by-product and only against large cuts. Q-learners enforce collusion only in pricing. Prompted LLMs reach cartel-like outcomes mostly through rules that ignore the market. Outcome measures cannot tell these cases apart; the audit can.

entry.title: How to Use Parallel Data for Multilingual Pretraining [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.28838v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-quality human-translated parallel corpora can improve cross-lingual transfer, but are typically too small for large-scale pretraining. Machine-translated web corpora help overcome this limitation, making parallel data available at pretraining scale. Standard multilingual pretraining, however, samples source documents and their translations independently, without explicitly using their parallel structure. We investigate how to use the parallel structure of the data to improve multilingual pretraining by concatenating each document with its translation in the same training sequence. We compare this parallel pretraining (PPT) approach with standard pretraining (SPT), training models from scratch at matched token budgets. Surprisingly, despite the benefits of parallel data reported in prior cross-lingual work, PPT alone does not consistently improve language understanding over SPT. Our further analysis suggests that although PPT builds a strong cross-lingual foundation, as shown by its better use of shared information across languages, the mismatch between parallel training contexts and single-language task inputs limits its gains in general language understanding. This finding motivates a two-stage approach following the pretraining-fine-tuning paradigm: we first use PPT to build a cross-lingual foundation, then continue with SPT to adapt it to standard language modeling. In both high-resource and low-resource settings, the two-stage approach consistently improves general language understanding and cross-lingual task performance over standard pretraining alone at matched training budgets.

entry.title: KIRA: A Full-Stack Reading Screening System with Dual-Pathway Analysis for Children [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.28840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Early-grade reading screening is critical for identifying children at risk of reading difficulty. Existing AI-based screeners are often limited in the scope of their analyses and evaluation metrics, or are proprietary systems that lack transparent model specifications and evaluation. We present KIRA, a dual-pathway screening system that pairs word-level fluency scoring with detailed phoneme-level error detection. We adapt pretrained word and phoneme recognizers to children's speech, reducing word error rate from 13.88% to 8.84% and phoneme error rate from 41.66% to 23.00%. Powered by these child-adapted models, we implement Word Reading (WRE) and Oral Reading Fluency (ORF), two foundational tasks in K-2 screening. The system integrates these recognizers with a web-based teacher-facing interface presenting fluency scores alongside phoneme feedback for potential targeted intervention. KIRA brings modern child-speech recognition into a full-stack, deployable, classroom-ready reading screener.

entry.title: SANE: Automated Scorer-Specific Metamorphic Testing for LLM Judges [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.28886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM judges increasingly mediate benchmark evaluation, model selection, data curation, and training. Their decisions are useful only when each judge responds reliably to changes affecting its scoring criterion. Existing methods for reliability testing perturb inputs with known expected effects on judge scores. Prominent LLM-judge testing harnesses combine human-authored perturbation recipes with synthetic test generation, leaving scorer-specific recipe ideation outside the automated pipeline. This limits their use to fixed perturbations and pre-assumed scorer types. We introduce SANE, an agent-based framework that encodes behavioral requirements for stochastic evaluators as reusable agent instructions. Given a scorer specification, implementation, and representative inputs, the pipeline first identifies scorer-specific capabilities, then automatically derives perturbation recipes and expected score relations for each. SANE also defines a scorer-independent validation framework for generated judge tests. It determines whether each recipe agrees with scorer intent and whether each instantiated case realizes the recipe and supports its expected relation. Because SANE generates a recipe inventory tailored to each scorer, the number of aligned recipes grows as scorers are added. Across five domains, SANE produces 3.7 times as many validated test families as the Judge Reliability Harness (JRH) at comparable end-to-end validity and detects scorer deficiencies in every domain, including professionalism and toxicity, where JRH detects none. On faithfulness, SANE achieves strong human alignment in judge ranking: its test-suite scores rank 11 judge models consistently with human-labeled FaithBench performance (Spearman rho = 0.852), while JRH does not (rho = 0.100).

entry.title: CSD: Common-Support Distillation for Cross-Tokenizer Knowledge Transfer [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.28895v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cross-tokenizer logits distillation enables knowledge transfer across model families, allowing students to learn from stronger or more specialized teachers. However, differences in vocabulary and segmentation make teacher and student next-token distributions difficult to align. Existing logits-based methods are easy to integrate into standard distillation pipelines, but often rely on restrictive heuristics or tokenizer-pair-specific choices. They may restrict supervision to shared vocabulary subsets, require manually selecting different objectives for different tokenizer pairs, or match only the observed chunk and its complement rather than individual alternative continuations. We introduce Common-Support Distillation (CSD), a unified logits-based framework that constructs a shared support between the teacher and student at each aligned input chunk and matches the induced distributions with a single objective. For one-to-one alignments, CSD uses explicit common-token pairs as the shared support. For other alignments, it constructs a virtual support whose probabilities are computed using the autoregressive chain rule. A residual event captures probability mass outside the explicit support, ensuring that both induced distributions remain normalized. Across four teacher-student settings comprising Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma3-1B-PT students with Qwen and Phi teachers, CSD consistently achieves the highest average performance among the evaluated cross-tokenizer methods, outperforming the strongest alternative by up to 1.8 points and surpassing both continued pretraining and same-tokenizer distillation. For Llama-3.1-8B, CSD improves average accuracy over the strongest evaluated baseline by up to 4.2 points for the base student and 1.6 points for the instruction-tuned student.

entry.title: Is Refusal Direction Universal across Low-Resourced Languages? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.28897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Refusal directions have been shown to transfer cross-lingually with near-perfect effectiveness across safety-aligned languages (Wang et al., 2025), reportedly regardless of resource level. However, the only truly low-resourced language evaluated is Yoruba, which is strongly misaligned and shows limited transfer, leaving open how refusal directions behave for other low-resourced languages. We extend PolyRefuse to three additional low-resourced languages (Belarusian, Bashkir, and Tajik) and replicate the pipeline of (Wang et al., 2025) on Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct.
